messages.subject: Mitxture Model for Time Series.
parts:
I am trying to set up a mixture model in PyStan and I am not sure whether my approach is correct.

I have time series data and I want to fit several models, that may be nested.
I know that generally none of the models is able to capture all characteristics of the data.

I'd be interested in the posterior likelihood of the model parameters and the model choice,
in order to see how parameter across-model-means, weighted by the respective model likelihood, perform.
Therefore I was planning to do something along the lines of what John Kruschke describes as transdimensional MCMC.
Since this is not possible in Stan, what I want to do is mixture modelling as described in chapter 9 of the tutorial.

So, this is a simple version of it:

data {

    int<lower=1> K; // number of mixing components

    int<lower=0> N; // number of data points

    vector<lower=0>[N] aif;

    positive_ordered[N] time;

    vector[N] data;

}



parameters {

   simplex[K] w; //Mixing proportions
   // real<lower=0, upper=1> weight1; //alternative to simplex

    real<lower=0.01, upper=3> par1[K]; // model parameter

    real<lower=0.01, upper=.8> par2[K]; // model parameter
    real<lower=0> sigma[K]

}


model {

   real ps[K];

   ps[1] <- log(w[1]) + normal_log(data,

                    Model1(time, aif, par1, par2), sigma[1]);

   ps[2] <- log(w[2]) + normal_log(data,

                    Model2(time, aif, par1, par2), sigma[2]);

        increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));

   }


Model1 and Model2 are computationally fairly expensive, separately defined functions.

Does this approach make sense at all for this kind of model?
Is it ok to use normal_log on the vectors (model and data)?

The results I get for an easy test seem to be correct (see attachment, model paraemters were .7 and .2)
The only thing that confuses me is, that the wrong (in this example very wrong) model still
get's a fairly large mixture proportion (mean at about 30% of the right model), as shown in the attached graphical output.
I would have expected it to be close to zeros, and the w distribution to become more like a delta peak.
How should I interpret this mixing proportions? They don't seem to allow for something like a weighted mean estimate.

Thank you

This is the right way to define a mixture model if you want to generalize
beyond 2 components.

Whether the combination makes sense depends on the data and
what Model1 and Model2 are!
> Is it ok to use normal_log on the vectors (model and data)?

Yes. See the manual for how this works. If you have a data
vector y, mean vector mu, and sd scalar sigma, then

normal_log(y,mu,sd) = SUM_{n in 1:size(y)} normal_log(y[n], mu[n], sd);

So mu and y need to be the same size. And both must be vectors (not
matrices).

> The results I get for an easy test seem to be correct (see attachment, model paraemters were .7 and .2)
> The only thing that confuses me is, that the wrong (in this example very wrong) model still
> get's a fairly large mixture proportion (mean at about 30% of the right model), as shown in the attached graphical output.
> I would have expected it to be close to zeros, and the w distribution to become more like a delta peak.
> How should I interpret this mixing proportions? They don't seem to allow for something like a weighted mean estimate.
>

How much data did you have and what were the priors? It takes a lot
of data even to estimate a bernoulli as a sharp peak.

You should explore what the parameters are for model1 and model2 and
perhaps also save the log probabilities in each model and keep them
with the data points and you might see what's going on.

- Bob
